title: PWM
goals: Work out the duty cycle, on-time and average voltage of a PWM signal
Say why PWM wastes so little power, and why the frequency must suit the load
Set up time-proportioning control of a heater through a solid-state relay
Work out a PWM output's resolution from its clock and frequency
Say what a drive's carrier frequency changes
summary:
**Pulse-width modulation** (PWM) switches a supply fully **on** and fully **off**, quickly, and varies the fraction of time it is on: the **duty cycle**, $D = \frac{t_{on}}{T}$.

The **average** voltage is $V_{avg} = D V_s$: 24 V at 25% duty averages 6 V. Because the switch is always either fully on (almost no voltage across it) or fully off (no current), it wastes very little power: the reason PWM is everywhere.

The **period** is $T = \frac{1}{f}$, and the on-time $t_{on} = D \times T$.

The load must smooth the pulses: a motor by its inductance and inertia, a heater by its thermal mass, an LED by your eye. So the frequency must be well above what the load responds to: hundreds of Hz for LEDs, kilohertz for motors (above about 16–20 kHz to be silent), but only **seconds** for a heater through an SSR.

**Time proportioning**: a temperature controller's 0–100% output switches a **solid-state relay** (SSR) on for that share of a fixed **cycle time**: 40% of a 2 s cycle is 0.8 s on, 1.2 s off.

For a resistive load such as a heater, **power** goes with duty: $P = D\frac{V^2}{R}$. 50% duty is half power (not a quarter).

**Resolution**: a PWM made by counting a clock has $N = \frac{f_{clk}}{f_{pwm}}$ steps per period: more frequency, fewer steps.

A **low-pass filter** (an RC with a corner frequency far below the PWM frequency) turns PWM into a steady analogue voltage.

A VFD's inverter is PWM: it switches the DC bus at the **carrier frequency** (typically 2–16 kHz), varying the duty in a sine pattern so the motor current comes out nearly sinusoidal. A higher carrier makes the motor quieter but the drive hotter.
sources: Horowitz, P. and Hill, W.: The Art of Electronics, 3rd edition (Cambridge University Press): switching regulators and PWM
Kuphaldt, T. R.: Lessons in Electric Circuits and the Socratic modules (pulse-width modulation)
ABB: Technical guide book (drives: switching frequency, PWM inverters)

formulas.name: Duty cycle
formulas.says: The share of each period that the output is on.

formulas.name: Average voltage
formulas.says: Averaged over each period, the output is the supply times the share of time it is on.

formulas.name: Period
formulas.says: The time for one cycle is one over the frequency.

formulas.name: Power into a resistive load
formulas.says: The full power, for the share of the time it is on.

formulas.name: PWM resolution
formulas.says: A PWM counter steps once per clock tick, so the steps per period are the clock over the PWM frequency.
symbols: the number of steps in each period
formulas.example: 16 MHz clock, 20 kHz PWM: 800 steps (about 9.6 bits).

bench.task: Look at a PWM signal on an oscilloscope: a 12 V fan or LED strip driven from a small PWM controller, or a microcontroller pin. Low voltage only.
check: Measure the period across the screen and work out the frequency
Measure the on-time and work out the duty cycle
Change the setting and watch the on-time change while the period stays the same
Measure the average with a multimeter on DC volts: it should be close to duty × supply

cards.q: A 24 V supply is switched fully on and off very fast, on for a quarter of the time. What average voltage does a DC motor see?
cards.why: On for 25% of the time at 24 V, off the rest: the average is $0.25 \times 24 = 6$ V. The motor's inductance and inertia smooth the pulses into a steady speed.

cards.title: On, off, and the share of the time
cards.body:
**PWM** switches the supply **fully on** and **fully off**, many times a second, and varies how long it stays on in each period.

The **duty cycle** is the on share: $D = \frac{t_{on}}{T}$, written as a fraction or a percentage. The **average** voltage is

$$V_{avg} = D V_s$$

The switch is either fully on (almost no volts across it) or off (no current), so it wastes very little power, unlike a resistor or a transistor left half on.
cards.more:
Picture dimming a room by flicking the light switch on and off very fast. If it is on half of the time, the room looks half as bright, because your eye averages the flashes.

Numbers: 12 V at 40% duty is 4.8 V on average.

The old way was a series resistor or a transistor half on, dropping the rest of the voltage as heat: at 50% that wastes as much power as reaches the load. PWM wastes only the switch's small losses, which is why fan controllers, LED dimmers, battery chargers and VFDs all use it.

cards.q: A {vs} V supply is switched by PWM at {d}% duty. What is the average voltage?
cards.why: On for {d}% of the time at {vs} V, off the rest: the average is {d}% of the supply.
cards.hint: Duty as a fraction, times the supply.

cards.title: Frequency, period and on-time
cards.body:
The PWM **frequency** $f$ is how many periods a second. The **period** is $T = \frac{1}{f}$, and in each period the output is on for

$$t_{on} = D \times T$$

Changing the duty changes the on-time; the period stays the same.

Watch the units: at 20 kHz the period is 50 **µs**; at 1 kHz, 1 **ms**.
cards.more:
Numbers: 25 kHz at 40% duty. $T = 1 \div 25\,000 = 0.000040$ s = 40 µs. On for $0.4 \times 40 = 16$ µs, off for 24 µs.

A handy shortcut: 1 ÷ kHz gives ms. 1 ÷ 25 = 0.04 ms = 40 µs.

On an oscilloscope, the pulses stay the same distance apart as you turn the setting; only their width changes. That is the 'width' in pulse-width modulation.

cards.q: PWM runs at {f} kHz with {d}% duty. How long is each pulse on?
cards.why: The period first (1000 ÷ kHz gives µs), then the duty's share of it.
cards.hint: Period in µs = 1000 ÷ the frequency in kHz.

cards.title: The load does the smoothing
cards.body:
PWM only works if the load **averages** the pulses:

- a **motor**: its inductance smooths the current, its inertia the speed. Kilohertz; above about 16–20 kHz it is silent.
- an **LED**: your eye averages it. A few hundred Hz or more, or it flickers (worse on camera).
- a **heater**: its thermal mass averages over seconds or minutes, so an SSR switching every second or two is plenty.

Too **slow** for the load and it follows the pulses: flicker, hum, judder. Too **fast** and the switch's own losses grow.
cards.more:
Each load has a 'response time'. PWM must be much faster than it.

A DC motor's winding inductance means the current cannot change instantly, so at 20 kHz it ripples only slightly around its average. At 50 Hz the current would rise and fall each pulse, and the motor would buzz and shake.

At the other end, every switch-on and switch-off wastes a little energy while the transistor passes through half-on. Switch 100 000 times a second instead of 10 000 and that loss is ten times bigger.

So: as slow as the load allows without complaint, and no faster.

cards.q: A small DC motor driven by PWM at 2 kHz whines loudly. What change usually quietens it?
options: Raise the PWM frequency above about 20 kHz
Lower the PWM frequency to 50 Hz
Add a resistor in series with the motor
cards.why: The whine is the motor's windings vibrating at the PWM frequency. Above about 20 kHz it is beyond hearing. 50 Hz would buzz and judder; 100% duty just runs it flat out.

cards.title: Heaters: slow PWM through an SSR
cards.body:
A temperature controller (or PID block) works out an output from 0 to 100%. A heater cannot take an analogue signal, so the output is **time-proportioned**: a **solid-state relay** (SSR) is switched on for that share of a fixed **cycle time**.

40% of a 2 s cycle: on 0.8 s, off 1.2 s, repeat.

For a resistive load, power goes with duty: $P = D\frac{V^2}{R}$, so 40% duty is 40% of full power.
cards.more:
It is PWM with a period of seconds instead of microseconds. The heater's thermal mass smooths it out: the temperature barely notices each pulse.

The cycle time is a setting: shorter gives smoother control but more switching. SSRs switch at the AC zero crossing, so they can manage a cycle of a second or so for years. A mechanical contactor wears out, so with one the cycle time must be much longer (tens of seconds), which makes control rougher.

Note the power: the heater sees full voltage while on and none while off, so its average power is simply the full power times the duty. It is not $\frac{(DV)^2}{R}$, as it would be if the voltage itself were turned down.

cards.q: A PID output of {d}% drives an SSR with a cycle time of {ct} s. How long is the SSR on in each cycle?
cards.why: Time proportioning: the on-time is the output's share of the cycle time.

cards.title: Resolution: how fine the steps are
cards.body:
A microcontroller or PLC makes PWM by **counting** a clock. Each period is a number of clock ticks; the on-time can only be a whole number of them. So the number of steps in each period is

$$N = \frac{f_{clk}}{f_{pwm}}$$

Raise the PWM frequency and there are **fewer** steps: coarser control. In bits, the resolution is $\log_2 N$.
cards.more:
Numbers: a 16 MHz clock making 1 kHz PWM: 16 000 steps, about 14 bits. Making 20 kHz: 800 steps, about 9.6 bits. Making 100 kHz: only 160 steps.

So there is a trade-off: a silent motor wants a high PWM frequency, but fine speed control wants many steps. A faster clock gives both.

$\log_2 N$ is 'how many bits fit': $2^{10} = 1024$, so 800 steps is just under 10 bits.

cards.q: A PWM counter runs from a {clk} MHz clock and makes PWM at {fp} kHz. How many duty steps are there in each period?
cards.why: Clock ticks per PWM period: the clock frequency over the PWM frequency (watch MHz against kHz: a factor of 1000).

cards.q: A 12 V fan is driven by PWM at 25 kHz and 40% duty. Find the period, the on-time, the off-time and the average voltage.
cards.why: Period from the frequency, then shares of it. 25 kHz is above hearing, so the fan is quiet.

cards.q: Why does the period stay at 40 µs whatever the duty is set to?
cards.context: 25 kHz PWM: T = 40 µs at 40% duty, and at any other duty.
cards.model: The period is set by the PWM frequency alone: 25 000 periods a second, so each one lasts 40 µs. The duty only decides how much of each period is spent on. Turning the duty up widens the on-pulse and shortens the off-gap by the same amount, so the period stays the same.
points: Duty splits the period into on and off

cards.q: A 3 kW heater is time-proportioned through an SSR with a 2 s cycle. The controller asks for 65%. What is the on-time, and the average power?
cards.why: Time share for the on-time; and since the heater sees full voltage while on, power share equals time share.

cards.q: A {kw} kW heater is time-proportioned at {d}% duty. What is its average power, in kW?
cards.why: Full voltage while on, nothing while off: the average power is the duty times the full power.

cards.q: Working out the on-time of 10 kHz PWM at 30%. One line is wrong. Which?
lines: So the pulse is on for 0.3 ms
cards.fix: Period: $\frac{1}{10\,000} = 0.0001$ s (100 µs), so the pulse is on for 30 µs
cards.why: One over ten thousand is 0.0001, not 0.001: a slip of a factor of ten. Check: 1 ms is a period of 1 kHz, not 10 kHz.

cards.q: Raising a VFD's carrier (switching) frequency from 4 kHz to 12 kHz makes the motor quieter. What is the main cost?
options: More switching losses: the drive runs hotter
The motor runs at a lower speed
The output voltage drops by two-thirds
The motor's torque is limited to a third
cards.why: Each switching event loses a little energy in the drive's transistors, so three times as many switchings mean more heat; drives are often derated at high carrier frequencies. Higher carriers can also raise leakage currents through long motor cables.

cards.q: A microcontroller has no analogue output. How can a PWM pin make a steady 0–3.3 V signal?
options: Add an RC low-pass filter well below the PWM frequency
Add a resistor in series with the pin
Raise the PWM frequency to 1 GHz
It cannot: PWM is always on or off
cards.why: An RC filter with its corner frequency far below the PWM frequency averages the pulses into a steady voltage of duty × 3.3 V, with a little ripple. A buffer (op-amp) after it can then drive a load.

cards.q: A PWM output has {n} steps per period. What is its resolution in bits?
cards.why: Bits = $\log_2$ of the number of steps: $2^{bits} = N$.

cards.q: LED panel lights dimmed by PWM at 100 Hz look fine to the eye but flicker badly on a phone video. What helps?
cards.why: A camera samples the light many times a second and catches the gaps the eye averages out. PWM at several kilohertz or more leaves no visible gaps.

cards.q: A {r} Ω heater element on {vs} V is driven at {d}% PWM duty. What is its average power?
cards.why: While on, it has the full voltage and full power; while off, none. So the average power is duty × full power. Using the average voltage ($D V_s$) in $\frac{V^2}{R}$ would give $D^2$: too low.
cards.hint: Full power first, then the share of time it is on.

cards.q: PWM averaging {vavg} V across a {r} Ω resistive load: what is the average current?
cards.why: For a plain resistor, average current is average voltage over resistance: Ohm's law works on averages. (Power is the one that needs care: it does not follow the average voltage squared.)

cards.q: Match each load with a sensible PWM frequency.
pairs: A cycle of a second or two
A few kilohertz to about 16 kHz
cards.why: Slow enough to keep switching losses down, fast enough that the load smooths the pulses.

cards.q: 12 V PWM at 75% duty. Average voltage?
{f} kHz PWM at {d}% duty. On-time per period, in µs?
cards.why: Period in µs is 1000 ÷ kHz; the on-time is the duty's share of it.

cards.q: SSR cycle {ct} s, output {d}%. On-time?
cards.why: Time proportioning: the output's share of the cycle.
